items.title: chore(scripts): delete the object hashing library benchmark
items.body: `scripts/benchmark-object-hashing/` was added in March 2026 to pick a stable object hashing strategy: it compared `merkle-reference` against DAG-CBOR, `object-hash`, `hash-it`, and a stable-stringify baseline, and it compared three SHA-256 implementations underneath `merkle-reference`. The comparison had to cover Deno, Node, and a browser, because the fastest SHA-256 a server can reach is not available to a browser, so the same test data and the same table of strategies were written out three times: a Deno version, a hand-ported Node version, and a version written inline in a page, with a headless Chrome driver and a one-line wrapper alongside them. That question is closed. The repository no longer uses any of the libraries it weighed; values are hashed by `packages/data-model`'s `value-hash.ts` on top of `packages/content-hash`, and nothing in the workspace declares `merkle-reference` as a dependency. Hashing performance is now tracked by benchmarks that live in those two packages, where a change to the hasher is what runs them. The rig had also stopped working and stopped being true. Its Deno entry point imports `packages/data-model/value-hash.ts`, a path that moved under `src/` in May 2026, so module resolution fails and neither the Deno entry nor its wrapper can run; nobody noticed for over two months. The Node and browser variants still run, but they load pinned early-2026 versions of the abandoned libraries from a public CDN at run time and never included this repository's own hasher, so what they measure answers no live question. The documentation was worse than stale: it told the reader that `merkle-reference` is the production hasher, configured in a `packages/memory/reference.ts` that no longer exists. Nothing referred to the directory. Its five files were the only matches in the tree; the benchmarks workflow lists its bench files one by one and never included it, and no task invoked it. So the whole directory goes, and the finding it produced is kept as a record instead of as a runnable rig. The new document under `docs/history/` describes what was compared, over which shapes of data, and the two conclusions that outlived the libraries: choose the SHA-256 implementation per environment rather than fixing one, and prefer a canonical encoding to a full Merkle tree. It says plainly that the numbers printed in the deleted documentation were a sample of the output format rather than measurements from any recorded run, so a reader does not mistake them for a baseline. One stale pointer is fixed in passing. The verifiable-execution foundations spec sent readers to `packages/memory/HASHING.md` for the hashing rule, and that file is gone too. It now names the project's own `hashOf()` — which is what the same document's conventions section already said it uses — and links to the byte-level specification in the space-model formal spec.

items.title: bench: fix W1/W2/W4 output mismatches and implement real W5
items.body:
## Summary

Stage B / W5 measurements on the v0.2.0-niche / v0.3.0-negative tag were comparing **different programs** on BT-IS and SCALAR, so the instruction ratios did not measure the architectures on equivalent work. This PR rewrites all four workloads so BT-IS and SCALAR produce identical output on a fair comparison, then implements the canonicalization flagship that PLAN_6_STEPS_STATUS.md Step 3 called for but was never actually run.

## Honesty gate

`benchmarks/stage_b_word.py` and the new `benchmarks/stage_b_w5.py` **assert output equality** before reporting any instruction-count ratio. If BT-IS and SCALAR don't produce the same output, the script exits non-zero and prints FAIL. The old version of `stage_b_word.py` counted ops without checking outputs.

## Workload results (after fix)

| Workload                | BT-IS | SCALAR | ratio | output match |
|-------------------------|------:|-------:|------:|:------------:|
| W1 rotations            |     9 |     14 | 1.56x |   yes        |
| W2 voxel_count (3 alive) |   34 |     52 | 1.53x |   yes        |
| W4 cubeadd_loop (10x)   |    32 |     22 | 0.69x |   yes        |
| W5 48 O_h inner loop    |   281 |    384 | 1.37x |   yes        |

Pre-correction numbers in `docs/STAGE_B_RESULTS.md` and `docs/STAGE_W5_RESULTS.md` (1.40x, 0.85x, 1.47x, 0.67x) were on mismatched programs. The honest numbers above are different: BT-IS wins on three workloads, loses on one.

## Why W4 changed sign

The previous W4 measured different recurrences:
- BT-IS: `C := C + mem[C]` (the cube_add primitive as defined). After iter 0, C's address changed so `mem[C]` was empty and subsequent iterations were no-ops.
- SCALAR: `C0 := C0 + C0` (always real work).

This rewrite makes BT-IS do `C := C + C` directly using D0 to hold the running operand and refreshing it after each `cube_add`. The honest ratio is 22/32 = 0.69x: BT-IS is **slower** on the pure cube-add primitive when both compute the same recurrence. The 1.47x headline was an artifact of comparing different programs.

## W5 was a 7-term composition, not canonicalization

The previous `programs/w5_compose.btis` and `benchmarks/w5_scalar.py` claimed to test the canonicalization flagship ("apply all 48 O_h elements, pick the lex-minimum"). They actually tested a single 7-term composition followed by one apply. The PLAN-recommended canonicalization experiment was never run.

This PR implements the **inner loop of canonicalization** on a single cube:
- Generate the 48 O_h permutations (24 proper + 24 improper).
- Verify group axioms: bijectivity, closure over all 2304 pairs, negation maps proper to improper.
- For each permutation, factor it into a minimum-length sequence of named BT-IS rotor ops (BFS; max factor length: 3).
- Emit the BT-IS program and a SCALAR equivalent.
- Assert both produce the same 48-output orbit (each of 6 axial states x 8).

W5 honest result: **BT-IS 1.37x faster** on setup cost. BT-IS loads a permutation into R0 in 0-3 named `rot_*_r` / `reflect_*_r` / `neg_r` instructions, then `apply_r 0`. SCALAR has no cube-copy primitive, so it must rebuild the input cube from scratch each iteration using 3 LOAD_IMM + 3 CGET = 6 ops. Both architectures pay 1 op for the apply itself.

## What this does NOT prove

- The original 48x canonicalization claim was for an `apply_r_to_mem` opcode that operates on a 27-cell pattern. That opcode does not exist in the current ISA. The current `apply_r` is one permutation applied to one cube, so the 27x outer factor cancels out. The 1.37x win is the setup cost only.
- The full W1/W2/W4/W5 work does not establish a general BT-IS advantage; it's mixed (3 wins, 1 loss on a fair comparison).
- The new honest ratios supersede the v0.2.0-niche and v0.3.0-negative numbers in `docs/RESULTS.md` and `VERDICT.md`. A follow-up commit will update those documents.

## Files added

- `benchmarks/stage_b_w5.py`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/oh.py`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/verify.py`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/factor.py`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/factor_sequences.json`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/gen_w5_btis.py`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/oh_perms.json`
- `benchmarks/w5_canon/w5_scalar.py`
- `programs/w5_canon.btis`

## Files modified

- `benchmarks/scalar_vm_word.py` (add REFLECT_X/Y/Z constants)
- `benchmarks/stage_b_word.py` (output-equality gate)
- `benchmarks/w1_word_scalar.py` (mirror BT-IS sequence)
- `benchmarks/w2_word_scalar.py` (fix register bug, 3-alive pattern)
- `programs/w4_cubeadd.btis` (rewrite for C := C + C)
- `programs/w2_voxel_count.btis` (rewrite to match SCALAR)
- `docs/STAGE_W5_RESULTS.md` (rewrite to describe the real 48 O_h workload)

## How to verify

```bash
git checkout v0.3.1-fixes
python3 benchmarks/stage_b_word.py
python3 benchmarks/stage_b_w5.py
```

Both should exit 0 with all four workloads reporting OK and a ratio column.

## Out of scope for this PR

The original review surfaced other issues that are not addressed here:
- Stage A programs (`gcd.btis`, `life3d_step.btis`, `sort3x3x3.btis` are still stubs)
- Turing-completeness proof (assumes unbounded memory that does not exist)
- VM/assembler bugs (silent operand default, register-mask bounds check, BR_AXIS unreachable, undo_all incomplete)
- Verilog core (most opcodes are TODO stubs; area/timing claims are projections, not measurements)
- Documentation drift (CHANGELOG, README, prompts reference stale numbers and counts)

These should be addressed in separate PRs.

items.title: [processor/dynamic_sampling] move buffered spans at decision time instead of copying
items.body:
#### Description

Companion to #50026, applied to the decision path. `assembleTrace` deep-copied every buffered ResourceSpans into the output at decision time, and profiling showed that copy was ~52% of decision-path allocation bytes. The buffered spans are processor-owned (created fresh in `ConsumeTraces`) and the pending trace is discarded after the decision, so they can be moved instead. `readIncomingSampling` reads the same spans and already runs before assembly; a comment now pins that ordering and `finishDecision` nils the consumed slice.

Also fixes two benchmark issues found while measuring:

- The incoming-tracestate decide benchmark used an `rv` of 16 hex digits (the spec requires exactly 14), so it exercised the parse-failure path and understated real tracestate cost.
- `BenchmarkDecide` reused one pendingTrace across iterations, which breaks once spans are consumed; it now rebuilds the trace per iteration (untimed).

Benchmarks (Apple M4 Pro, mean of 5 runs, measured after the benchmark fixes so before/after are like-for-like):

| BenchmarkDecide case | ns/op before | ns/op after | Δ | B/op before | B/op after | Δ | allocs/op before | allocs/op after | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1span_catchall | 1,931 | 1,436 | -26% | 1,272 | 648 | -49% | 24 | 13 | -46% |
| 10spans_catchall | 4,523 | 3,102 | -31% | 7,392 | 3,320 | -55% | 105 | 49 | -53% |
| 10spans_catchall_incoming_tracestate | 7,852 | 6,721 | -14% | 8,272 | 4,200 | -49% | 135 | 79 | -41% |
| 10spans_5ottl_rules | 6,677 | 5,424 | -19% | 8,042 | 3,967 | -51% | 145 | 89 | -39% |
| 100spans_catchall | 27,739 | 16,044 | -42% | 68,688 | 29,960 | -56% | 915 | 409 | -55% |
| 100spans_5ottl_rules | 44,015 | 34,277 | -22% | 75,174 | 36,416 | -52% | 1,315 | 809 | -38% |
| 1000spans_catchall | 264,149 | 150,837 | -43% | 680,791 | 296,364 | -56% | 9,015 | 4,009 | -56% |
| 10000spans_catchall | 2,435,400 | 1,163,242 | -52% | 6,802,536 | 2,960,366 | -56% | 90,015 | 40,009 | -56% |
| 10000spans_5ottl_rules | 4,084,604 | 2,673,498 | -35% | 7,444,723 | 3,602,399 | -52% | 130,018 | 80,011 | -38% |

#### Link to tracking issue
Refs #49311

#### Testing

- Full suite passes with the race detector; existing decide/eviction/late-span tests cover the consumed-spans semantics.
- Before/after benchmark comparison across all `BenchmarkDecide` cases (numbers above).

#### Documentation

Comments on `assembleTrace` and `finishDecision` documenting the move semantics and ordering constraint. Changelog entry included.

#### Authorship

- [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself.

items.title: docs(benchmarks): fix "larger m" claim and add three RESULTS caveats
items.body:
## Motivation

A review of `benchmarks/` found the evidence provenance **essentially perfect** — every number in `RESULTS.md` re-derives from the committed CSVs (all of Tables 1–8 checked by hand), the simulation is statistically valid (`β̂ = R·β + chol(R)·u/√n`, i.e. the correct `N(Rβ, R/n)` sumstat model), and SD/SE labeling is honest. This PR closes the few gaps the review surfaced. **Documentation only — no committed benchmark numbers change.**

## Changes

**Fix the "larger m" description-vs-artifact mismatch.** `rg_polygenicity.py`'s docstring and `benchmarks/README.md` described the committed polygenicity run as being at a "larger m", but the committed `rg_polygenicity.csv` uses the **default** geometry (m = 5,000; `n_causal = 500` at p = 0.1). Reworded both to state the committed run is m = 5,000, with a larger m available via the `MUT_RATE`/`K` env vars.

**Add three caveats near the RESULTS headline** (all grounded in the committed CSVs):
- **In-model vs real-genotype.** The rg-accuracy wins (Sections 1–4) are measured with exactly the `N(Rβ, R/n)` noise the bivariate likelihood assumes — favourable ground for a model-based estimator vs moment-based LDSC. The one out-of-model, real-genotype test (Section 7) is where the `cross_corr` correction is *not* reliably recovered, so "halves LDSC's error" is an in-model result and doesn't automatically transfer to raw real-genotype sumstats.
- **High-rg attenuation.** LDpred3 shrinks high true rg downward (at rg = 0.95: 0.906 infinitesimal, 0.922 polygenic, 0.938 moderate — straight from `rg_architectures.csv`), the expected bias–variance trade behind its tighter SD.
- **Section 1 exclusion asymmetry.** The LDSC MAE/SD exclude `|r̂g| > 1.5` replicates (the `ldsc_fail` column; one dropped rep in `major_locus` at rg = 0.95) while LDpred3's are never excluded — so the comparison, if anything, flatters LDSC and the LDpred3 win is conservative.

**CHANGELOG** entry under `[Unreleased] → Fixed`.

## Testing

- Documentation/docstring only; no code or CSV changed. `ruff check bipred tests benchmarks` clean.
- Cited numbers verified against the committed CSVs (`rg_architectures.csv` rg=0.95 rows; `rg_polygenicity.csv` n_causal).

## Note on CI

CI will be red on the pre-existing private-ldpred3 install issue (the runner can't clone the private dependency without the `LDPRED3_TOKEN` secret) — unrelated to this doc-only diff. That plumbing already merged (workflow is ready); it just needs the secret.

items.title: release: 2.4.1
items.body:
Aligns everything on one version. The benchmark tooling that keeps ranks instead of verdicts, and the corrected headline table, were sitting on `main` while PyPI still served 2.4.0 with a README describing weights the library no longer ships. Anyone arriving from the package page got the stale text.

## In this release

**Added**
- The LongMemEval checkpoint records the rank of every evidence and gold-session hit, plus each question's evidence count. Any smaller k, and the strict "every flagged turn retrieved" reading, become recomputable from a finished run instead of requiring another six-hour pass.
- `engram-bench longmemeval` prints turn recall three ways: any flagged turn retrieved, the same over questions that flag any turn at all, and every flagged turn retrieved.

**Fixed**
- The published turn-recall figure now carries the caveat it needed: 21 of the 500 questions flag no turn and cannot be hit (over the 479 answerable ones the figure is 0.866 at k=5, not 0.830), and 59% flag more than one, so "at least one retrieved" is an upper bound on what the model was handed.
- The headline recall table said `hybrid` (default) over the figures for `0.7 / 0.3`, which stopped being the default in 2.4.0 itself.

## Behaviour

Unchanged. The additions are to the benchmark harness; the fixes are to what the documentation says about numbers that were already there. Patch release.

## After merge

`v2.4.1` gets tagged, which publishes, and a GitHub release page follows so the repository, PyPI and the README all show the same version with nothing lagging behind.

items.title: Pre-launch number audit: two wrong numbers, one restored section
items.body:
## What this PR does

A full pre-launch pass: every quantitative claim in the README and docs re-measured against a fresh run of the actual benchmark scripts, rather than trusted from memory.

**Two numbers were wrong:**

- *"Our benchmark shows graph memory preserves +5% more information than a summary baseline"* — the real, currently-measured delta is **+10 points** (89% vs 79%), matching every other mention of this same benchmark. The +5% was never updated after the underlying number moved.
- A resume block averaging **"249 tokens"**, cited in two places as *"measured, n=3"* — re-running `benchmarks/checkpoint_accuracy/runner_v2.py` today gives **178 tokens** (197 / 193 / 144 across the three sessions). A third, unrelated "247 tokens" attached to a *fictional* worked example in `docs/architecture.md` was measured against nothing — removed rather than replaced with another fake-precise number.

**Also fixed:**
- `docs/api.md` carried the MCP registry's `mcp-name:` ownership marker as bare visible text instead of an HTML comment — rendered as a stray, out-of-place line in the middle of the MCP setup instructions. New guard test.
- `TESTING.md` described a "no network access" audit environment from an early debugging session that no longer exists, and claimed 23 stdlib tests where the script now runs 25. Rewritten to describe the current suite (600 tests) instead of a frozen historical snapshot.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s project-structure tree said "42 files" for `tests/`; actual count is 44.
- Persist-latency and label-quality numbers in `docs/benchmarks.md` refreshed against a clean run on this machine.

**Restored "Why TokenMizer and not X?" to the README.** It answers Git history, RAG, plain summaries, Mem0/Zep, and a longer context window — and had been moved into `docs/comparisons.md` during the documentation split, one click away from the page most likely to be the first thing a new reader scrolls past. Phase 1 of the mem0-parity plan — the agent-facing **memory-management surface** that mem0's MCP has and Anamnesis lacked. Ships as **0.12.0**.

## Added
- **5 MCP management tools**: `update`, `forget` (soft-retract + `hard` flag), `supersede`, `list`, `get` — the agent can edit, forget/delete, mark-outdated, browse, and inspect memories. `relate` also accepts `supersedes`.
- **Kernel/framework**: `Relation::Supersedes`, `Engine::unretract`, and a `Memory` management API (`update_content`/`get`/`list`/`forget`/`unforget`/`delete_hard`/`supersede`) with `MemoryView` + `ListFilter`.
- **remember** gains optional `tags`/`metadata`/`scope`; **list**/**recall** support tag/metadata/scope filtering (recall filters the rendered context package, not just candidate ids).

## Fixed
- **Extraction queue is now per-namespace** (was a single global queue) — captured turns no longer leak across projects; a non-default namespace's backlog is rebuilt on first open after a daemon restart.
- README benchmark numbers reconciled to the calibration-records SSOT.

## Changed
- Internal: `dispatch.rs`/`memory.rs` split into submodules (behavior-preserving).

Public API changes are **purely additive** (new types/methods + a non-exhaustive variant) -> minor bump.

1151 workspace tests green (`cargo nextest run --all-features`), clippy `-D warnings` clean, doctest + doc clean, fmt clean.

items.title: docs: correct benchmark dataset hierarchy — wiki_all_1M canonical, Cohere legacy (#92 redefined)
items.body:
## Summary

Implements the **redefined** scope of #92 (see the [2026-08-04 redefinition
comment](https://github.com/pg-cuvs/pg_cuvs/issues/92#issuecomment-latest) on
the issue) — the original acceptance ("regenerate the Cohere CSV with
non-zero `index_bytes`") is **withdrawn**. This is documentation/ledger work
only: no GPU, no benchmark reruns, no measured numbers changed.

> 재정의 근거 (issue #92, 2026-08-04): "기준은 이미 wiki_all_1M(cuvs-bench 표준,
> data.rapids.ai)로 옮겨갔다... 대외 커뮤니케이션도 이미 이동했다(2026-07-24 NVIDIA
> 메일은 §2.1b를 인용)... 원래 acceptance는 철회한다 — 해당 결함은 코드 수정
> (#75/#79)으로 이미 해소됐고 그 증거가 wiki1m canonical 산출물이다. 결함 CSV는
> 재측정 대상이 아니라 은퇴 대상이다."

The docs described the project's dataset hierarchy backwards relative to
actual practice: `BENCHMARK.md` declared Cohere 1M×1024 "Primary dataset" and
"canonical" (§2.1a) while carrying a known `index_bytes=0` defect, and
demoted the wiki_all_1M cross-machine reproduction (§2.1b) — the dataset
NVIDIA's 2026-07-24 email and #98 actually cite — to a "reproduction"
footnote.

## Changes (3 commits, split by intent)

1. **Artifact rename + ledger** — `bench/results/pg_cuvsbench_1m.csv` →
   `pg_cuvsbench_1m_legacy.csv` (`git mv`); `bench/results/README.md` ledger
   row updated to `legacy` status with a one-line defect note (was a 17-line
   block); wording states the fix (#75/#79) and canonical wiki_all_1M rows
   as the corrected evidence.
2. **BENCHMARK.md / README.md hierarchy** — §0 "Primary dataset" → wiki_all_1M
   (Cohere relabeled "Legacy dataset"); §2.1a heading/framing: canonical →
   "legacy dataset (Cohere)", scoped as "canonical within the Cohere lineage"
   where that's still accurate (it's the fix lineage for the k-wiring/
   VRAM-accounting defects); §2.1b promoted to canonical. README's benchmark
   section now leads with the wiki_all_1M ~5.4× citation (existing §2.1b
   number, not a new measurement) and demotes the Cohere table to a labeled
   legacy comparison — its own ratios (~4.5× search, ~2× build) are **not
   deleted**, just relabeled per dataset.
3. **Reference sweep** — every live doc naming the old filename or implying
   Cohere-as-primary: `ROADMAP.md` (#92 release-readiness row rewritten for
   the redefined scope; the dated ADR-080 completion entry gets its filename
   updated in place, narrative untouched), `bench/cuvs_bench_backend/README.md`
   + `run_pg_cuvsbench.py` (usage examples), `design/benchmarks/crossover-methodology.md`
   (filename + rename pointer in an existing baseline-reconciliation note).

## What I deliberately did NOT touch

- **`design/specs/phase-record.md:1201`** — `docs/doc-map.md` states it is
  frozen history ("Do not reopen ... it is frozen history"). Left as-is; it
  still names the old filename in a historical evidence line, which is
  accurate as written (it was true at the time).
- **`design/decisions.md` ADR-080 body** (evidence table, numbers, `데이터
  정합성 정정` note) — append-only per `docs/doc-map.md`. Added a short dated
  addendum after the existing block, matching the doc's own precedent for
  self-correction notes (the existing 정정 note at the same ADR), recording
  the hierarchy change without rewriting the original evidence.
- **Ratio claims** (~4.5×/~5× search, ~2× build) — same-run comparisons,
  kept as valid; only the primary/canonical *dataset* label moved.

## Investigation note: `pg_cuvsbench_1m_guarded.csv`

The issue mentioned a "ledger-unregistered byte-identical duplicate"
`pg_cuvsbench_1m_guarded.csv`. I confirmed it is **byte-identical** to the
original `pg_cuvsbench_1m.csv` (`diff` clean), but it is **not tracked by
git anywhere in history** on any branch — it exists only as an untracked
local file in one contributor's working directory. There is nothing to
rename/remove in this repo; no action taken here. Worth a heads-up to
whoever has that local file, but out of scope for this PR.

## Verification

- `bash scripts/docs-contract-check.sh` → `[OK] documentation contract
  checks passed` (run after every commit).
- No `src/` changes, no code behavior changes (the two `.py` docstring/
  comment edits are example `--out` paths only).
- `grep -rn "pg_cuvsbench_1m\.csv"` (excluding `_legacy`) across the repo
  now only matches `design/specs/phase-record.md` (frozen) and the original
  evidence block inside `design/decisions.md`'s ADR-080 (intentionally
  preserved, append-only).

## Test plan

- [x] `scripts/docs-contract-check.sh` passes
- [x] All new/changed relative links point at files that exist
      (`pg_cuvsbench_1m_legacy.csv`, `pg_cuvsbench_wiki1m.csv`,
      `pg_cuvsbench_wiki1m_brev.csv`)
- [ ] CI green (Tier-1) — watching after push

Relates to #92 (redefined scope). This PR intentionally does **not** close the issue,
per the task instructions; leaving that to the issue owner to confirm intent
was fully captured.

items.title: fix(backtest): honor explicit local source for engine routing and benchmark

## Summary

- Route data sources without a dedicated engine branch (e.g. `local`) by detected instrument market, so a local `AAPL.US` dataset gets `GlobalEquityEngine` US-equity rules instead of the `CryptoEngine` default.
- Fetch explicit benchmarks through the configured source's loader first, keeping yfinance as the fallback, so `source: local` backtests stay offline and reproducible.

## Why

Engine routing in `_create_market_engine` fell through to the crypto default for any source without its own branch, and `resolve_benchmark` always created a `YfinanceLoader`, ignoring the configured source. Closes #550.

## Changes

- `agent/backtest/runner.py`: market-based routing (US/HK equity → `GlobalEquityEngine`) in the source fallback branch.
- `agent/backtest/benchmark.py`: `resolve_benchmark`/`_fetch_benchmark` accept the source's loader and try it before yfinance.
- `agent/backtest/engines/base.py`: pass the run's loader through; `source: auto` keeps the yfinance default.
- `agent/tests/test_local_source_routing.py`: routing + benchmark-forwarding regression tests.
- `CHANGELOG.md`: entry under Unreleased → Fixed.

items.title: perf(vm): JIT J4c — variable-op helper hot paths: gated marker probes, symbol-keyed reads (ADR-0004 J4)
items.body:
## Summary

Third J4 slice. After J4b put `int-arith`'s loop body on the JIT, the profile showed the remaining per-iteration cost was **not arithmetic but the variable-op helpers**: `format!`-built env marker keys, per-read `Symbol` interning, and ungated metadata probes. This fixes them at the interpreter level, so **both modes benefit**.

| fix | what it removes (per iteration in an int loop) |
|---|---|
| `CheckReadOnly` marker probes gated on process-global "ever created" flags (extends the existing `CLOSURE_META_KEY_SEEN` chokepoint in env.rs) | 2× `format!` alloc + 2× env lookup per whole-variable assignment |
| `GetGlobal` fast scalar read via the memoized `const_sym` | per-read intern; **and the `_`→`-` kebab re-probe: `"_"` contains an underscore, so every `$_` read ran the whole fallback chain twice** |
| `GetLocal`/`SetLocal` ContainerRef-adoption probe via `code.locals_sym` | per-op re-intern of the local's name |
| `distribute_bound_multidim_slice` gated on a `__mutsu_bound_array_slice::` flag | `format!` + env probe + String/holder clones per scalar assignment |
| `resolve_binding` empty-map fast exit | hash of the name per GetLocal |

Soundness of the flags: monotonic and process-global, set at the single String-keyed `Env::insert` chokepoint every creation site flows through; an over-set only makes the (correct) probe run — same argument as the existing `CLOSURE_META_KEY_SEEN`. The `GetGlobal` fast path's gates reproduce the slow chain's precedence, and Nil / LazyThunk / ContainerRef hits fall through to the unchanged slow tail.

## Also

- **`scripts/bench-ci.sh`**: every benchmark now also measured with `MUTSU_JIT=on` as its own `<bench>+jit` series (same TSV schema) — JIT-mode history accumulates on `bench-data` from the next main push.
- **CLAUDE.md**: documentation numbers come from the bench CI history (`bench-data`), citing the commit hash; local `perf stat` A/B stays for PR descriptions only.

## Verification

- `make test` green (JIT off); full `prove t/` green with `MUTSU_JIT=on MUTSU_JIT_THRESHOLD=2`.
- Touched-semantics pins green: S03-binding roast ×7 + assign ×2 + variables-and-packages, `t/sigilless-params.t`, `t/array-bind-cell.t`, `t/cas-multidim-cells.t`, `t/multidim-delete-after-ephemeral-block-coherence.t`, ...
- All benchmark outputs byte-identical JIT on/off.

## Measured locally (release, `perf stat -r5`, `taskset -c 0-3`; CI numbers land on `bench-data` after merge)

| bench | J4b baseline | J4c | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| int-arith, JIT off | 90.0 ms | 59.6 ms | **−34%** |
| int-arith, JIT on | 79.7 ms | 52.8 ms | **−34%** (≈0.39x of raku) |
| fib, JIT on | 116.1 ms | 110.3 ms | −5% |
| bench-fib, JIT on | 322.9 ms | 301.2 ms | −6.7% |
| method-call / bench-class, JIT on | — | — | −2〜3% |

items.title: ci: raise the docs build timeout to 90 minutes
items.body:
The docs build is running close enough to its timeout that a slower runner would start failing it.

## Numbers

The reusable `documentation.yml` defaults to `timeout_minutes: 45`, and this repo's caller does not override it.

Recent Documenter job durations:

| run | duration | share of cap |
|---|---|---|
| main, 12 Aug | 40 min | 89% |
| feat/product-ratio, 11 Aug | 27 min | 60% |
| fix/154, 11 Aug | 42 min | 93% |

All three passed. Two had under five minutes of headroom.

## Why it will bite

The build compiles the AD-backend tutorials and runs a full linkcheck.
Linkcheck is network-bound and variable — a local build already hit a transient `curl` timeout against a badge URL, which resolved on retry.

A timeout would present as an intermittent red rather than an obvious limit, which is the expensive kind to diagnose. Better to move the cap now than to spend a morning on it later.

## Why 90

Matches the cap already used for the benchmark job, and leaves room for the tutorial set to grow. The reusable's comment describes the input as being there so heavier docs builds can raise it, which is this case.

Raising a timeout does not make anything slower. It only changes when the runner gives up on a build that has genuinely hung.

## Managed file

`document.yaml` is scaffold-managed, but the kit explicitly supports this: a package may hand-add the `with:` block and `update()` preserves it across syncs.

This was opened by a bot. Please ping @seabbs for any questions.

items.title: bench(nfr04): parity suites vs pinned baselines, and the uniq/groupBy fix they found

milestone.title: M7 — Benchmarks & release readiness
milestone.description: NFR enforcement at full strength and the first public release Roadmap items: 7.1–7.6 (6 total).

items.body:
## Summary

Implements roadmap **7.1** — NFR-04 parity benchmarks against exactly-pinned lodash/p-limit/p-retry baselines — and **opens Milestone 7**. The roadmap flagged *"fair-comparison methodology is the hard part"*; it was, and it is recorded as **ADR-0013**.

**It also found and fixed a real NFR-04 violation**: `groupBy` and `uniq` were **2.0–2.7× slower than lodash**. See below.

## Motivation

NFR-04: *"retry/parallelLimit within 10% of p-retry/p-limit; data functions within 10% of lodash equivalents or faster."*

Producing numbers is easy; producing numbers that **mean** what the requirement intends is not — and a benchmark that measures the wrong thing is *worse than none*, because it converts a false claim into a green check.

## Three hazards, and what was done about each

**1. The async combinators are dominated by waiting, not code.** With default options a `retry` benchmark measures hundreds of ms of backoff and a concurrency benchmark measures the tasks — both libraries would score identically and "parity" would be a measurement of `setTimeout`. Delays are therefore zeroed on **both** sides (`minDelay/maxDelay: 0` for ours; `minTimeout/maxTimeout: 0, factor: 1, randomize: false` for p-retry) and tasks resolve immediately, so **orchestration overhead** is what is measured. The suite states in-file that this says nothing about real-world retry latency, which the caller's chosen backoff dominates.

**2. Same-named functions are not the same function.** Comparisons are against the equivalent **usage**:
- p-limit's `Promise.all(tasks.map(task => limit(task)))` wrapper sits **inside** the timed region — it is what a user writes to achieve one `parallelLimit` call.
- `lodash.merge` is called as `merge({}, a, b)`: it **mutates its target**, and crediting it for allocation it never does is the unfair direction.
- `uniq(array, fn)` is compared to `uniqBy`, not `uniq`.

**3. Where semantics cannot be equalized: disclose, and do not quote the ratio as a performance claim.** Merge appears **twice** — an **array-free** input (the NFR-04 figure, **6.9×**, because the divergence cannot arise there) and an **array-heavy** input kept because it is realistic but labelled **NOT A PARITY CLAIM**: its ~189× is the cost of doing *different work* (we replace a 40-element array, lodash deep-merges it element-wise). Also disclosed inline: lodash `omit`'s deep-path feature surface, our `groupBy`'s `Map` return, `deepClone`'s native `structuredClone` versus a JS walker.

Functions with **no baseline** (`validateEmail`, `parseDuration`, `urlSearchParams`, `uuid`, type guards) live in a separate suite carrying **no NFR-04 claim** — inventing an unlike comparison to publish a favourable number would be the dishonest version of this work. Inputs come from a **seeded PRNG at module load**, never `Math.random`, never inside a timed region. Baselines are pinned **exactly** (`lodash 4.18.1`, `p-limit 6.2.0`, `p-retry 6.2.1`): a drifting baseline makes a 10% comparison meaningless across runs. p-limit 6 / p-retry 6 are the last majors supporting the **Node 18 floor** (7.x needs ≥20; p-retry 8 needs ≥22).

## What the suite found — the point of having it

`groupBy` and `uniq` were **2.0–2.7× slower than lodash**, violating NFR-04. Diagnosis found two **accidental** costs, neither required by our semantics, both removed with **zero behaviour change**:

- `Array.prototype.forEach` with a closure → an indexed loop.
- `uniq` routed **every element through an identity function** even when no iteratee was supplied; the no-iteratee path now compares the element itself. `Set` still supplies SameValueZero, which is the documented contract.

| Row | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `groupBy` vs lodash | lodash **1.99× faster** ❌ | **egl 1.46× faster** ✅ |
| `uniq` vs lodash | lodash **2.68× faster** ❌ | **egl 1.45× faster** ✅ |
| `uniq(fn)` vs `uniqBy` | lodash **2.36× faster** ❌ | **egl 1.41× faster** ✅ |

All **594 tests and 100% coverage held** across the change.

## Measured position (single machine, indicative — the gate is 7.2)

| Comparison | Result |
|---|---|
| `retry` immediate success vs `p-retry` | **5.2× faster** (stable, gate-able) |
| `retry` 2 failures, zero backoff vs `p-retry` | **~parity** (±10% variance — indicative only) |
| `parallelLimit` 100@4 / 1000@16 vs `p-limit` + wrapper | **2.3× / 3.5× faster** |
| `deepClone` vs `cloneDeep` | **1.2× faster** |
| `deepMerge` vs `merge({}, a, b)`, array-free | **6.9× faster** |
| `pick` / `omit` vs lodash | **4.5× / 2.0× faster** |
| `groupBy` vs lodash | **1.5× faster** |
| `uniq` / `uniq(fn)` | **1.5× / 1.4× faster** |

## A finding that constrains 7.2

**Not every row can be gated at 10%.** The two-transient-failures retry row crosses timer boundaries and swings ~±10% between runs (observed 1.00×, 1.03×, 1.04×, 1.06×, and once 1.12× in p-retry's favour) — **its variance is the same size as the threshold**, so it is *indicative* only; parity is real but a 10% gate on it would flake nightly. The pure-overhead row is stable and gate-able. ADR-0013 records this so the nightly gate isn't designed against it and the constraint isn't rediscovered by a red build.

## Verification

- [x] `pnpm bench` runs the real suite (it was a placeholder), so the existing CI `benchmark` job executes it unchanged
- [x] `vitest bench` scoped explicitly to `src/bench/` — test and bench globs never overlap
- [x] `pnpm coverage` — **594/594**, **100%** coverage (unchanged by the optimization)
- [x] `pnpm lint` (eslint + `tsc --noEmit` strict checkJs), `pnpm check:package`, `pnpm format:check`, `python tools/consistency_lint.py` green

## Documentation Impact

- [x] ROADMAP.md checkbox flipped (7.1) + Spec Coverage Map §3/§6 rows updated
- [x] ADR added — **ADR-0013: Benchmark methodology — what counts as a fair comparison, and what we refuse to compare** (+ index row)
- [x] CHANGELOG.md — Changed (suite + methodology) **and Fixed** (the uniq/groupBy regression)

items.title: Docs/site review follow-up: consolidate benchmark numbers, merge ADR trees, fix page metadata
items.body:
Follow-up to a documentation/website/UX review of the current version. The theme throughout: numbers and status claims were maintained in several places at once and had drifted apart after the 1.4/1.5 releases. This PR removes the duplication so each fact has one source of truth, and fixes the technical issues the review surfaced.

## Benchmark numbers: one source of truth

- `docs/proof-and-benchmarks.md` and `README.md` no longer quote their own (stale, mutually inconsistent) copies of the e2e workflow medians — they link the checked report `benchmarks/e2e-workflow/results/latest.md` and `docs/benchmark-e2e-workflow.md` instead.
- The website compare page derives its medians from `site/app/data/bench.ts`, which the existing `verify-site-bench-data.mjs` guard already asserts against the checked report — so the previously drifted "174 ms / 2254 ms" cells can no longer go stale. Hero/ProofStrip ratios come from the same guarded data.
- Fixed the compare criterion label (the cited numbers are from the realistic corpus, not the small one) and the Ferrocat version note (2.2.0, matching the pinned crate).

## ADR trees merged

`docs/adr/` (001/002, added 2026-07-22) collided with the canonical `adr/` series (001–016), claimed canonical status in parallel, and was never published to the website — the hosted CLI plugin API pages linked into a void. The plugin ADRs are now `adr/017` and `adr/018`, `DECISIONS.md` indexes them, links on the API pages resolve to live `/decisions/*` routes, and hardcoded "16 ADRs" counts were either removed or (on the site) derived at build time.

## Website fixes

- **Missing page metadata (SEO):** ~120 of 126 prerendered routes had no `<title>`, description, canonical, or OG tags. Root cause: Ardo 4 injects meta in an `enforce: "pre"` transform that looks for the compiled `export const frontmatter` in *raw* markdown, so it never fires. A small post-phase Vite plugin in `site/vite.config.ts` now injects the meta export after MDX compilation (and becomes a no-op if Ardo fixes the ordering upstream). Verified in the build output.
- **Hosting matrix:** `matrix.ts` claimed Remix subdomain demos were live (they are not hosted). It now matches `docs/demo-deployments.md`: cookie, route, and subdomain live for the five browser-verified frameworks; tld stays `provisioning` (domains not provisioned yet); Remix cells link the verified source. The `/frameworks` prose and per-framework panels agree with the table on the same page, and the deployment doc intro now states the tld status unambiguously.
- **Derived stats:** ADR count and example-matrix shape ("24 apps", "6 × 4") are generated into `content-stats.json` during prebuild instead of hardcoded — on the home page and the frameworks page.
- Removed the stale checked-in `sitemap.xml` (6 URLs, shadowed by the generated 126-URL one) and duplicate `robots.txt`; the get-started "Read the docs" CTA now points at `/docs` instead of the API reference; blog lede extraction no longer uses "Status: draft" as the meta description.

## Docs fixes

- `examples/README.md`: all 29 root-relative links resolved to 404 on GitHub (`examples/examples/…`); now correctly relative. Same class of fix in `docs/demo-deployments.md`.
- Contradictory "five vs. six framework families" wording unified everywhere: six families, five browser-verified, Remix v3 smoke-verified.
- README no longer claims Remix is verified on Node `>=22.22` (the package requires `>=24.3`), and its 30-link "Proof And Adoption Docs" farm is reduced to the website entry points plus a handful of repo anchors.
- Quickstart (`first-working-translation.md`) now works from an empty directory: scaffold step, `react`/`react-dom`/`solid-js` in the install lines.
- `benchmark-lingui-v6-preview.md` no longer lists `msg`/`defineMessage` as covered syntax (removed from Palamedes in 1.5.0); `migrate-from-lingui.md` no longer shows a module-level `t()` call that the documented scope rule forbids.
- `llms.txt`/`llms-full.txt` catch up on the Remix adapter, the CLI plugin system, and ADR 017/018.

## API reference corrections

- `transform.md`: four catalog-loader helper signatures were outdated (e.g. `renderCatalogModule(artifact, options)` vs. the real `renderCatalogModule(messages)`); export list completed.
- `config.md`: documents `loadPalamedesConfigSync` (used by the Remix register hook).
- `core.md`: `getMessageNodes()` added to the `PalamedesI18n` snippet (custom implementations failed typecheck without it); missing node types listed.
- `remix.md`: `PalamedesRemixRegisterOptions` now shows `configPath`/`failOnMissing`/`failOnCompileError`; server accessor `get()` and the remaining `createRemixI18nServer` options documented.
- `runtime.md`: lists `ClientI18nSnapshot`.

## Verification

- `pnpm --filter @palamedes/site build` — green, including the bench drift guard, prebuild, Ardo link check (`level: "error"`), and prerender of all routes (now 128 with the two new decision pages). Spot-checked titles/canonical/OG in the built HTML and the rewritten `/decisions/017…` links on the hosted API pages.
- `pnpm --filter @palamedes/site typecheck`, `pnpm lint` (oxlint + eslint), `pnpm format:check` — all green.
- Greptile review findings (tld cells wrongly live, duplicated matrix counts) addressed in 9405053.

## Known issue, deliberately not fixed here

`benchmarks/e2e-workflow/src/corpus.mjs` still generates `defineMessage` imports for the **Palamedes lane** (lines 343/378). Since 1.5.0 removed deferred messages, regenerating the benchmark with a current CLI will likely fail or change results — the checked report was recorded with CLI v1.3.0. Fixing the corpus changes measured numbers, so it should be a separate, conscious change with a fresh report.

items.title: fix: align scanner rules with TypeScript reference
items.body:
## What changed

- groups contiguous full-width digits into one diagnostic while preserving the existing ASCII fix
- marks empty blockquotes as fixable and removes them
- reports blockquote spacing at the blockquote node start
- inserts a missing space after `>` and collapses multiple spaces to one
- replaces per-line blank counting with document-level leading, trailing, whitespace-only, and repeated-run semantics
- preserves LF, CRLF, and CR line endings
- keeps fenced-code lines protected from scanner fixes
- repeats fixes until stable so interacting rules converge on the TypeScript fixed output
- reduces the expected mismatch baseline from ten fixtures to the two parser-dependent inline-code fixtures
- updates the prototype rule documentation

## Why

The differential harness showed that most remaining mismatches were scanner semantics rather than parser architecture. The pinned TypeScript rules group `[０-９]+`, locate blockquote diagnostics at the node start, normalize both missing and multiple blockquote spacing, remove empty blockquotes, and report one document-level diagnostic per blank-line range.

## Scope boundary

This PR deliberately leaves `no-empty-inline-code/exact` and `no-empty-inline-code/whitespace` in the baseline. Those cases depend on Markdown inline-code parsing semantics and should not be approximated further in the scanner-only layer.

## Expected compatibility result

- 15 fixtures total
- 13 exact matches
- 2 known parser-dependent mismatches

## Validation

CI runs Rust format, Clippy, and tests on Linux, macOS, and Windows, followed by the pinned TypeScript–Rust differential harness and benchmark smoke checks.

items.title: feat(serving): benchmark scripts + fix 512 persistent concurrent streams
items.body:
## Summary

Add deterministic, reproducible benchmark scripts for NeMo ASR serving and fix the RNNT pipeline slot limit that capped persistent WebSocket connections at 256 — now verified at **512/512 concurrent streams for 10 minutes with 0 failures** on a single L4 GPU.

**Model:** [Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming 0.6B](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b) (0.6B params, cache-aware RNNT)
**GPU:** NVIDIA L4 (24 GB VRAM) · **Container:** NGC NeMo 26.02 (PyTorch 2.6 + CUDA 12.8)

---

## Benchmark Scripts

Four self-contained scripts using LibriSpeech test-clean with [Whisper English normalization](https://github.com/jianfch/whisper-normalizer) for WER:

| Script | Mode | Measures |
|--------|------|----------|
| `bench_batch.py` | Batch (REST) | WER, concurrency sweep, sustained load, smart mode |
| `bench_stream.py` | Streaming (WebSocket) | WER, concurrency sweep, sustained load, smart mode |
| `bench_stream_longlive.py` | Persistent/rotating | Connection stability, VRAM growth, TTFB, diverse audio |
| `eval_wer_detailed.py` | Verification artifact | Per-utterance WER with S/I/D breakdown |

All scripts auto-download LibriSpeech, run warmup, and output structured JSON + markdown.

---

## Server Fixes

### 1. RNNT Pipeline Slot Limit (root cause of connection drops)
`cache_aware_rnnt.yaml` hardcodes `num_slots=256`, but `max_concurrent_streams=512`. Streams 257+ got `"No free slots available"` error and were disconnected.

**Fix:** Pass `max_concurrent_streams` from serving config as `streaming.num_slots` when building the pipeline.

| Metric | Before (256 slots) | After (512 slots) |
|--------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Active at 60s | 192/512 | **512/512** |
| Active at 600s | N/A | **512/512** |
| Slot errors | 335 | **0** |
| VRAM baseline | 6714 MB | 8250 MB |
| VRAM peak | 11328 MB (leak) | 8672 MB (stable) |

### 2. GPU Work Queue Overflow
`_MAX_GPU_QUEUE=512` overflowed at c=512 (512 streams each submitting chunks). Raised to 4096.

### 3. uvloop Auto-detection
Auto-detect and use [uvloop](https://github.com/MagicStack/uvloop) for ~2-4x event loop throughput. Falls back to default asyncio if not installed.

### 4. WebSocket Ping Disabled
uvicorn's default `ws_ping_interval=20s` kills connections under GPU load — the event loop is too busy to handle ping/pong. Set to `None`; audio chunks serve as implicit keepalive.

---

## Benchmark Results

### Quality (WER)
| Concurrency | WER | Dataset | Normalization |
|:-----------:|:---:|:-------:|:-------------:|
| c=1 | **3.21%** | LibriSpeech test-clean | Whisper English |

### Streaming Concurrency Sweep (L4, rotating mode)
| c | RTFx | sess/min | Failures |
|:-:|:----:|:--------:|:--------:|
| 32 | 10.32x | 79.2 | 0 |
| 64 | 13.05x | 100.2 | 0 |
| 128 | 18.76x | 144.0 | 0 |
| 256 | 27.55x | 211.4 | 0 |
| 512 | 38.69x | 297.0 | 0 |

Still scaling linearly at c=512 — no ceiling hit.

### Persistent c=512 (L4, 2,620 unique LibriSpeech files, 10 min)
| Checkpoint | Active/Total | VRAM |
|:----------:|:------------:|:----:|
| 60s | **512/512** | 6456 MB |

items.body:
## What

Replaces every `[TBP]` placeholder across the SOTA/performance tables with **independently verified numbers** — not copied from the results summary at face value, but recomputed from the raw per-sample telemetry and cross-checked against every chart. Also closes the last of B3 (two docs still carried the old fabricated-title-style citations already fixed in `README.md`).

`scripts/results/` (JSON telemetry, PNGs, the corrected summary) is un-gitignored and committed — the docs now embed images and link data files from it, so it needs to actually exist in the repo for anyone else.

## Verification methodology

Every headline number was **independently recomputed from the raw 1000-sample / 88-probe arrays** in `benchmark_results.json` (not trusted from the summary doc) and cross-checked pixel-for-pixel against the PNGs. All matched exactly: intent accuracy (85.7%), full 4×4 confusion matrix, ToM MAE (0.032/0.041), Recall@K (81.8/87.5/87.5/93.2%), resource footprint (1,266 MB / 0.99 W), paralinguistic precision (95.3%/94.4%).

## Two fabrication bugs found and fixed (not just documented)

In `scripts/research/cognitive_metrics_eval.py`:
1. **`module3_memory_actr()`** silently fell back to `np.random.seed(42)`-generated **synthetic** latency-scaling numbers whenever real progression data was missing — that fabricated curve (flat 15ms vs. rising to 50ms) is what `cognitive_rag_recall.png`'s right panel actually plots. The real underlying data tells a much smaller story (~170ms→174ms vs. ~170ms→181ms, ~4% apart). **Fixed to raise instead of fabricate.**
2. **`module4_conflict_resolver()`**'s barge-in "stop latency" (104.3ms mean, 7.72ms std) was fake Gaussian noise (`np.random.normal`) sprinkled onto a real composed constant, and the "baseline" 479.9ms was a fully invented, uncited number. **Fixed to report the composed constant directly, with its provenance, and no fabricated baseline.**

## Also caught (labeling error, not a script bug)

The results summary attributed "162.79ms mean inference" to a local Qwen model. That figure is actually `memory_store.search_memories()` wall-clock time (traced through `hard_benchmark.py`), not LLM inference. **Retracted** rather than propagated into any doc.

Also: two different eval scripts model the Neo4j "standard database" comparison baseline as two different **unbenchmarked, arbitrary multipliers** (6.5-22× vs. a hardcoded fallback reached via a JSON key-path bug). Table III now carries the real cached/uncached numbers with this caveat explicit, and leaves "Performance Speedup" unfilled rather than publish a multiplier computed against an invented baseline.

## What's honestly left unfilled

Speech-to-Speech TTFT, Memory Scaling Complexity, and most of Table II's per-component rows are `*(not yet measured)*` — no defensible real number exists for them yet. "Accelerated" mode columns are marked `(mode retired)`: `hard_benchmark.py` explicitly refuses to run it ("disabled as requested by the user").

- `README.md` §8 + Performance SLOs, `backend/app/agents/context.md`, `docs/ROBOTICS_ANALYSIS.md`, `academic_benchmarks/documentation/{sota_comparisons,academic_sota_benchmarks,walkthrough}.md` — populated with verified numbers, footnoted by provenance.
- `.agents/CONTEXT.md` — new dated ledger entry documenting the verification pass and both fabrication bugs.
- `scripts/research/cognitive_metrics_eval.py` — the two bug fixes above.
- `scripts/results/*` (17 files, ~4.6MB, newly tracked) + `.gitignore` — committed so cross-references resolve.
- **B3**: `academic_sota_benchmarks.md` + `walkthrough.md` — vendor citations reclassified as product materials (not fake technical reports), one HippoRAG title correction, a stale-dataset-mirror warning fixed (was pointing at 97-byte placeholder stubs predating the real benchmark run).

items.title: ci(bench): nightly NFR-04 gate enforcing a parity floor, not a history diff

milestone.title: M7 — Benchmarks & release readiness
milestone.description: NFR enforcement at full strength and the first public release Roadmap items: 7.1–7.6 (6 total).

items.body:
## Summary

Implements roadmap **7.2** — the nightly NFR-04 gate. It enforces the requirement **as written**: a **floor** of `0.9` on `ourHz / baselineLibraryHz`, not a diff against stored history. Design and the measurements that forced it: **ADR-0014**.

Also corrects a defect in the merged 7.1 work — see the last section.

## How the design was arrived at (three implementations, two discarded)

ADR-0013 closed 7.1 with a warning: one comparison's run-to-run variance was the size of the threshold, so gating it would flake. Building the gate turned that warning into the central problem, and each attempt was killed by measurement rather than by taste:

**Attempt 1 — gate single-run ratios, guarded by vitest's `rme`.** Flaked immediately: **1–3 spurious failures on every run against unchanged code**. The diagnosis is the useful part: `rme` was ±1% while the ratio moved 15% *between* runs. **`rme` measures sampling precision, not reproducibility** — it looks like a noise estimate and describes the wrong noise, which made it worse than no guard at all.

**Attempt 2 — derive the gated subset from measured stability** (gate only rows whose spread is under the threshold). Honest, and it worked — but it enforced just **3 of 13** comparisons on this machine, and promoted or demoted rows depending on which 5-run sample happened to be tight, *including promoting the very row ADR-0013 had established as unstable*. That was the signal that the **quantity being compared** was wrong, not the statistics.

**Final — enforce a floor.** NFR-04's "more than 10% worse" means worse than the baseline **library**, not worse than our own previous run. A change leaving us 5× faster than lodash is not an NFR-04 violation. The floor makes noise irrelevant by construction: ratios sit at **1.2–6.7** while the floor is **0.9** — an order of magnitude of headroom that only a real defect crosses.

Along the way: the per-run distribution turned out to be **bimodal**, not noisy-around-a-mean (`uniq`: 2.35, 2.40, 2.40, then 1.44 — V8 settling into a slower tier). No threshold fixes a bimodal distribution; that observation is what ruled out tuning attempt 1.

## What ships

- **10 of 13 comparisons enforced**, with three exclusions, each recorded in the baseline file with its reason:
  - the **array-heavy merge** — its ratio is a difference in *work*, not speed (ADR-0013);
  - **parallelLimit settle mode** — no baseline library to normalize against;
  - the **timer-bound retry row** — the one comparison whose true value is *genuine parity* (~1.0), so it sits **at** the floor rather than far above it, and its ±10% swing has been observed at **0.85**. Parity there is real and verified by the 7.1 suite; it simply cannot be gated at a 10% tolerance.
- **Median of several passes** (median, not best-of-N: best-of-N discards unfavourable samples and would bias every number in our favour).
- `docs/benchmarks/baseline.json` is a **record for reviewers, not a gate input**. Drift is reported and never fails — so the gate has no bootstrap problem, and a stale record degrades a log line rather than the build. Observed drift on unchanged code was **−17% … +5%**, all reported, none failing.
- **Benchmarks gained explicit warmup.** Needed for the numbers to be *truthful* regardless of gating: the short defaults never let V8 finish optimizing either side, so the suite had been comparing two half-warm functions.
- Workflow: `benchmark-nightly.yml`, schedule `17 3 * * *` (off the hour) + `workflow_dispatch`, Node 20 to match the existing `benchmark` job, `--frozen-lockfile` because a differently-resolved baseline would change every ratio, output uploaded as an artifact.

## Verification

- [x] **The gate is proven non-vacuous, not assumed.** Re-introducing the exact inefficiency 7.1 found (`forEach` + an identity call per element in `uniq`) drives the ratio to **0.364** and fails the gate. Restored and re-verified clean (`git diff` empty).
- [x] **The gate does not flake.** Full run on unchanged code passes with all 10 enforced comparisons above the floor.
- [x] `pnpm coverage` — **594/594**, **100%** coverage
- [x] `pnpm lint`, `pnpm check:package`, `pnpm format:check`, `python tools/consistency_lint.py` green

## A correction to merged 7.1 work

ADR-0013 and the 7.1 changelog entry both asserted the baselines were **pinned exactly**. They were not: `pnpm add -D -E` with range specifiers (`lodash@4`) wrote carets, so **the documentation was ahead of the manifest**. Now pinned exactly, with Dependabot `ignore` rules added so a baseline bump is a deliberate re-baselining rather than a routine merge.

This is folded into this PR rather than split out because a **reproducible baseline is a prerequisite of the gate**, not unrelated cleanup — a gate measured against a drifting baseline would be exactly the kind of false green check this PR exists to avoid.

## Documentation Impact

- [x] ROADMAP.md checkbox flipped (7.2) + Spec Coverage Map §3/§6 rows updated
- [x] ADR added — **ADR-0014: The nightly NFR-04 gate — enforce a parity floor, not a diff against history** (+ index row), recording all three attempts and why two were discarded
- [x] CHANGELOG.md — the gate, and the pinning correction
- [ ] README.md — performance numbers land with 7.5's documentation pass
- [ ] Spec — no divergence
- [x] PR metadata set — assignee, `ci` label, `M7 — Benchmarks & release readiness` milestone

## Note

The nightly workflow cannot run on this PR (schedules only fire on the default branch). After merging, it is worth triggering it once via **workflow_dispatch** to confirm it is green on CI hardware — the runner is noisier than a dev machine, and the floor was chosen with that in mind, but confirming beats assuming.

items.title: fix(mcp): tolerate JSON-string list/dict arguments from MCP clients
items.body:
## Summary

- MCP tools with list/dict-typed parameters reject JSON-**string** arguments sent by some MCP clients — e.g. `run_shadow_backtest(markets='["us"]')` fails with `Input should be a valid list [type=list_type, input_value='["us"]', input_type=str]`.
- Attaches a pydantic `BeforeValidator` to every list/dict MCP parameter so a JSON-encoded string is decoded before validation. The published schema is unchanged, so well-behaved clients are unaffected.

## Why

FastMCP publishes optional list/dict parameters as `anyOf` schemas. Several MCP clients (observed with Claude Desktop / Claude Code) do not surface `anyOf` to the model as a concrete type, so the model serializes the array/object argument as a JSON **string**. Strict pydantic validation then rejects the call before the tool body runs:

```
1 validation error for call[run_shadow_backtest]
markets
  Input should be a valid list [type=list_type, input_value='["us"]', input_type=str]
```

Consequence: `markets` cannot be passed over MCP at all, and — combined with the default all-markets universe — `run_shadow_backtest` cannot be scoped to a single market, so one unreachable data source fails the whole run. The same rejection affects every list/dict MCP parameter.

I reproduced the exact error over MCP stdio, and confirmed the server already emits a typed `anyOf` schema across fastmcp 3.0/3.2/3.4 (the `{}` in the report is the client's rendering of `anyOf`). The robust, client-agnostic fix is therefore lenient input handling at the MCP boundary, as suggested in the issue.

Closes #987

## Changes

- `agent/mcp_server.py`:
  - Added `_coerce_json_string`, a pydantic `BeforeValidator` that decodes JSON array/object strings (`'[...]'` / `'{...}'`) and passes everything else through untouched (real containers, `None`, numbers, and non-JSON strings — the latter still hit pydantic's normal, precise type error).
  - Defined lenient `Annotated` aliases and applied them to all **13** list/dict parameters across **9** tools: `start_research_goal` (`criteria`), `add_goal_evidence` (`symbol_universe`, `benchmark`, `assumptions`, `contradicts_claim_ids`), `update_research_goal_status` (`audit`), `analyze_options_payoff` (`legs`, `scenario_iv_values`), `run_swarm` (`variables`), `get_market_data` (`codes`), `get_fund_flow` (`codes`), `get_stock_profile` (`sections`), `run_shadow_backtest` (`markets`).
  - The published JSON schema is byte-identical to before; real arrays/objects keep working.
- `agent/tests/test_mcp_json_string_args.py`: new regression suite (15 tests) — a schema guard (no regression to `{}`), helper unit behaviour, and end-to-end coercion through `fastmcp.call_tool` for both an optional `list[str]` and a required `list[dict]` param.

Risk note (agent-authored change): MCP-boundary only. No changes to protected areas, broker connectors, credentials, or order paths; every affected tool is read-only / research-only.

## Test Plan

- [x] Existing tests pass (`pytest --ignore=agent/tests/e2e_backtest --tb=short -q`)
- [x] New tests added (if applicable)
- [x] Tested manually (describe below)

items.title: docs: refresh benchmarks and docs for the 1.0.2 re-bench
items.body:
## Intent The developer was running the post-1.0.2 re-benchmark matrix (three arms: databricks-axi, cli-skills built from databricks/databricks-agent-skills, and mcp-aidevkit) and monitoring its progress, then updating the project docs to reflect the new results. Along the way they made explicit methodology decisions: drop the cli-skills repeat count from 5 to 3 for parity with the other arms, discard a 93-minute stalled cell as infrastructure noise, and permanently fix the recurring sql-count-aws failure caused by a UTC-vs-local, date-relative fixture rather than reseeding it daily. They wanted to confirm the arena already reflected the cli-skills swap, capture a fresh arena screenshot for the README, and ship the BENCHMARKS.md and README changes through the no-mistakes gate now that release-please had been removed, checking that no shipping instruction still referenced release-please. The final committed change was a small consistency fix: link the databricks-agent-skills repo in the README (and BENCHMARKS.md) the same way ai-dev-kit is linked, for parity. ## What Changed - Rewrote `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` and the README benchmark section around the post-1.0.2 three-arm matrix (databricks-axi v1.0.2, cli-skills, mcp-aidevkit), updating headline cost/turns tables, token counts, per-task rows, the 227-of-228 pass count, and methodology notes (26 tasks x 3 repeats plus 2 once-only mutating tasks per condition). - Linked the `databricks-agent-skills` repo in both README and BENCHMARKS the same way `ai-dev-kit` is linked, and replaced the arena screenshot (`docs/images/arena.png`) with a refreshed capture reflecting the cli-skills arm. - Reworded the AGENTS.md benchmarker role from "raw `databricks` CLI and MCP" to "competing CLI and MCP setups" to match the re-benched arms. ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: Documentation-only change whose benchmark numbers I verified are internally consistent (cell/pass counts, win-rate claims, and averages all reconcile) with no stale methodology references and all file links resolving. ## Testing Baseline `pnpm test` already passed (it includes the arena parse tests that cover the cli-skills condition wiring). On top of that I validated the documentation intent directly: the README and BENCHMARKS headline tables are numerically consistent with each other, the databricks-agent-skills repo is linked at parity with ai-dev-kit in both files, the arena UI and its tests already reflect the cli-skills swap, and no active shipping instruction still references release-please (only historical notes remain). I rendered both docs to HTML for reviewer-visible evidence and visually confirmed the refreshed arena.png shows the three arms with databricks-axi winning cost and turns. I could not produce a screenshot of the rendered README/BENCHMARKS because headless Chromium is missing a system shared library (libnspr4.so) that I cannot install under the workspace boundary; the rendered HTML files and the arena PNG serve as the visual artifacts instead. Overall: change works as intended, no findings. - Evidence: Refreshed arena screenshot (README hero image) showing CLI+agent-skills / MCP / databricks-axi, axi lowest cost & fewest turns (local file: /tmp/no-mistakes-evidence/01KXK6P9CDD3K0QZ7880ERK9Y8/arena-refreshed.png)
Evidence: Rendered README.md (Benchmarks section, headline table, both repo links) ```text

databricks-axi

Token-efficient Databricks CLI for AI agents, implementing the AXI standard (Agent eXperience Interface): TOON output, minimal default schemas, structured errors, contextual next steps, ambient context.

Wraps the official databricks CLI. Auth, transport, and API coverage stay upstream; this tool reshapes the experience for agents.

One task, three agents, one workspace, via the arena demo you can run yourself. A demo, not a benchmark: one run each, no repeats, no grading. The measured numbers are in docs/BENCHMARKS.md.

Why databricks-axi

An agent working with Databricks today has three options, and each has a real cost. The raw databricks CLI returns human-shaped text: bare confirmations, inconsistent formatting, no hint at what to do next. The agent has to parse prose and often re-run a command just to see what happened. Databricks' workspace-managed SQL MCP server returns structured output, but it is a small server that still loads a full tool schema into context every session, and it is confined to SQL: it cannot trigger a job run or touch anything outside that surface, so it ends up querying system tables to triage a failed job instead of just asking the jobs API. Databricks Field Engineering's ai-dev-kit MCP server covers the full surface, close to 40 tools, but pays for that coverage with the largest schema load of any option here.

AXI is a set of interface design principles for CLIs meant to be driven by agents rather than humans: structured output, minimal schemas that expand only on request, and ambient context so a command answers "what should I do next" as well as "what happened." The premise is that a CLI built this way can match an MCP server's structure and reliability without paying an MCP server's schema tax on every session.

databricks-axi applies those principles to the official databricks CLI instead of replacing it. Auth, transport, and API coverage stay upstream; this tool only reshapes output and interaction: TOON instead of raw text, structured errors instead of stack traces, contextual next steps instead of silence, and enough ambient context that the agent doesn't need a follow-up question to know where it is. Because the jobs and SQL surfaces live behind the same CLI, triaging a failed run stays a jobs-API call, no system-table workaround needed. See Benchmarks below for how that plays out in cost and turns.

What the agent sees

Same workspace, same question, both CLIs. The raw CLI:

$ databricks jobs list -o json
[
  {
    "created_time": 1700000000000,
    "creator_user_name": "you@example.com",
    "job_id": 123456789012345,
    "settings": {
      "email_notifications": {},
      "format": "MULTI_TASK",
      "max_concurrent_runs": 1,
      "name": "nightly-etl",
      "queue": {
        "enabled": true
      },
      "timeout_seconds": 0
    }
  }
]

databricks-axi:

$ databricks-axi jobs list
jobs[1]{job_id,name,creator_user_name}:
  123456789012345,nightly-etl,you@example.com
count: 1
help[2]: databricks-axi jobs view <job_id>,databricks-axi jobs runs <job_id>

TOON rows instead of nested JSON, a minimal default schema (--fields expands it), and the next two commands an agent would reach for. Errors follow the same contract:

$ databricks-axi catalog table view workspace.default.does_not_exist
error: "Error: Table 'workspace.default.does_not_exist' does not exist."
code: NOT_FOUND
help[1]: databricks-axi catalog tables workspace.default

Exit code 1, a stable code field, and the recovery command. Nothing to parse out of prose, nothing to guess.

Benchmarks

Agent ergonomics is measurable. A bench run compared databricks-axi against two competing setups on real Databricks tasks (list jobs, triage a failed run, read a table schema, cycle a cluster, and similar): databricks-axi (v1.0.2), cli-skills (the official databricks CLI v1.6.0 plus the databricks-agent-skills skill pack, pinned 5bc462d4), and mcp-aidevkit (Databricks Field Engineering's ai-dev-kit stdio MCP server, pinned a7e1d51). The agent was claude-sonnet-5, running each task cold in its own session against two live workspaces (AWS serverless, AWS2 classic clusters).

227 of 228 published cells passed (99.6%): databricks-axi 80/80, cli-skills 80/80, mcp-aidevkit 67/68. The one failure, clusters-view-aws on mcp-aidevkit (1 of 3 repeats), is a real gap in that tool's cluster-read call: it omits node type, DBR version, and autotermination for a TERMINATED cluster, not a databricks-axi issue. Since databricks-axi and cli-skills both pass 100%, the cost and turns comparison below is apples-to-apples on task success.

Cost and turns are the headline metrics, not tokens: cost_usd is Claude Code's own billing-correct total, weighted by the real cache-read discount (~0.1x). Over the 24 tasks and 68 cells every condition ran:

Condition Avg Cost Avg Turns vs axi (cost / turns)
databricks-axi $0.143 3.1 baseline
cli-skills $0.249 6.8 +75% / +118%
mcp-aidevkit $0.201 4.3 +41% / +39%

databricks-axi wins or ties on cost in 51 of 52 task/condition comparisons and on turns in 49 of 52.

Input-side tokens (input + cache-write + cache-read) tell a similar story but run 85-87% cache read on these cells, which bills at roughly 0.1x, so a raw token count overstates the real cost gap by about 1.3x. Reported here for reference, not as the lead number: databricks-axi averages 113,613, cli-skills 230,449, mcp-aidevkit 172,830.

The reason is structural. cli-skills layers agent-skill documents on top of the raw CLI's output, and loading a skill body adds real turns and tokens on top of parsing the CLI's plain text. mcp-aidevkit loads close to 40 tool schemas into context every session. databricks-axi exposes the same surface as a single CLI the agent already knows how to read, with a minimal default schema and no skill body or tool list to load.

Full per-task numbers live in docs/BENCHMARKS.md.

To watch the comparison live against your own workspace, the repo ships a local demo: node tools/arena/server.mjs runs one task of your choosing three ways (CLI + agent-skills, MCP, databricks-axi) side by side. It is a demo, not the benchmark; see tools/arena/README.md.

Requirements

  • Node.js >= 20
  • Official databricks CLI >= 0.298, authenticated (databricks auth login --host <workspace-url>, or DATABRICKS_HOST/DATABRICKS_TOKEN env vars)

Usage

No install needed:

npx -y databricks-axi            # ambient home view
npx -y databricks-axi --help

Cold npx resolution is a one-time cost on that first bare run; once databricks-axi setup hooks installs the session-start hook, every hooked agent session invokes the installed binary directly and pays none of it.

Install the Agent Skill (Claude Code and compatible harnesses):

npx skills add p33ves/databricks-axi --skill databricks-axi -g

Roadmap

v1 command surface (see the AXI standard for the principles each follows):

Domain Verbs
home ambient context dashboard ✅
jobs list, view, run, runs, logs, cancel ✅
clusters list, view, start, stop ✅
sql warehouses, exec, statement view, history ✅
catalog catalogs, schemas, tables, table view, volumes, volume view, functions, function view ✅
workspace ls, view ✅
fs ls, cat ✅
pipelines list, view, start, stop, events ✅
serving list, view ✅
api raw REST passthrough ✅
setup hooks install (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) ✅
whoami caller's own identity (SCIM Me): user, groups, entitlements ✅

Development

corepack enable
pnpm install
pnpm test
pnpm run lint && pnpm run format:check
pnpm run build:skill   # regenerate skills/databricks-axi/SKILL.md

See CONTRIBUTING.md. Contributions ship through no-mistakes.

Security

See SECURITY.md. Secret values are never accepted as flags, and tokens are never echoed. Authenticate with the least-privilege profile or token the task needs; don't reach for an admin/all-workspaces profile for a read-only or single-object task.

License

MIT

```
Evidence: Rendered docs/BENCHMARKS.md (methodology, results, per-task tables) ```text

Benchmark results

Full detail behind the numbers in the README, for anyone who wants the per-task breakdown instead of the headline average.

Methodology

Real Databricks tasks (list jobs, triage a failed run, read a table schema, cycle a cluster, and similar), each run cold in its own session by claude-sonnet-5, against two live workspaces: AWS (serverless, data/jobs/notebook fixtures) and AWS2 (classic clusters). Tasks cover operational read/diagnose/status work, not authoring workflows.

Three conditions:

  • databricks-axi @ v1.0.2, this tool
  • cli-skills: the official databricks CLI v1.6.0 plus the databricks-agent-skills skill pack, pinned 5bc462d4
  • mcp-aidevkit: Databricks Field Engineering's ai-dev-kit, a stdio MCP server covering jobs/clusters/SQL/UC/pipelines/serving, pinned a7e1d51. It gets its normal MCP connection warm-up time before the task starts, matching how a person would use it interactively.

26 tasks x 3 repeats, plus 2 once-only mutating tasks, per condition. mcp-aidevkit doesn't run 4 workspace/fs tasks (notebook-read, notebook-discovery, api-current-user, fs-error-recovery); those rows read — for it. Success is graded deterministically where the answer is machine-checkable, by an LLM judge otherwise.

cli-skills' agent instructions hand-feed the router step that tells the agent to load the matching product skill, even though this arm ships no router hook of its own. Deliberately generous: its numbers below are a floor on its real overhead, not a ceiling.

databricks-axi and cli-skills both pass 100%, so the cost and turns comparison below is apples-to-apples on task success.

mcp-aidevkit $0.201 4.3 +41% / +39%
